title: substring bounds
explanation: Half-open ranges [start, end) are everywhere in Java: substring, copyOfRange, subList. The length is always `end - start`.

title: Letter index
prompt: Complete the classic count-array idiom for lowercase letters.
explanation: 26 slots for a-z; `c - 'a'` maps 'a'→0 ... 'z'→25. This exact loop opens Valid Anagram and many others.

title: Predict the output: chars and ==
prompt: Predict exactly what each line prints.
explanation: `char + int` is int arithmetic: 'a' is 97, so 98 prints. Casting back to `char` gives 'b'. With a String on the left, `+` concatenates → `a1`. `new String("hi")` is a distinct object, so `==` (same reference?) is false while `equals` (same characters?) is true.

title: Keep letters and digits, lowercased
prompt: Return `s` with every character that isn't a letter or digit removed, and all letters lowercased. E.g. `"A man, a plan!"` → `"amanaplan"`. Use `Character.isLetterOrDigit`, `Character.toLowerCase`, and a `StringBuilder`.

solution.explanation: One pass: filter with `isLetterOrDigit`, lowercase with `toLowerCase` (which leaves digits unchanged), append to a StringBuilder so the build stays O(n).

hints: Walk the characters once, deciding for each whether to keep it — and in what form.
`Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)` decides whether to keep a char; `Character.toLowerCase(c)` is safe to call on digits too.
Append kept chars to a `StringBuilder`, then return `sb.toString()`.

title: Sum a comma-separated list
prompt: `s` is a non-empty list of integers separated by commas, like `"3,10,-2"`. Return their sum. Use `split` and `Integer.parseInt`.

solution.explanation: `split(",")` produces the number strings; `Integer.parseInt` handles the minus sign. A string with no commas splits into one piece. O(length of s).

hints: First break the text into pieces, then turn each piece into a number.
`s.split(",")` gives a `String[]`; loop over it.
`Integer.parseInt(part)` converts `"-2"` to `-2`.

title: Drill: sorted-character key
prompt: From memory: return the characters of `s` sorted ascending, as a String. `"tea"` → `"aet"`. Three lines: `toCharArray`, `Arrays.sort`, `new String`.

solution.explanation: Strings are immutable, so copy to a `char[]`, sort that in place, and build a new String from it. Anagrams always produce the same key. O(k log k) for a string of length k.

hints: You can't sort a String directly — get a mutable array of its characters first.
`s.toCharArray()`, then `Arrays.sort` on that array.
Turn the sorted array back into text with `new String(chars)` — not `chars.toString()`.

title: Why StringBuilder
prompt: Building an n-character string with `result += c` in a loop is O(n²). Why?
options: Strings are immutable, so each += copies the entire string built so far
The += operator is slow for all types
The garbage collector runs after every +=
It isn't — the compiler optimizes it to O(n)
explanation: Each concatenation allocates a fresh string and copies 1+2+...+n ≈ n²/2 characters total. StringBuilder appends into a growable buffer: O(n) overall.

title: Count the vowels
prompt: Return how many characters of `s` are vowels (`a e i o u`, lowercase input). Loop with `charAt`, or `toCharArray()` with an enhanced for.

solution.explanation: Visit each char once and count matches — O(n). `"aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0` is a compact alternative to the chain of ==.

hints: Look at each character once and keep a counter.
chars compare with `==` (they're primitives): `c == 'a' || c == 'e' || ...`.

title: Drill: reverse a string
prompt: From memory, two idioms in one: convert to `char[]`, two-pointer swap in place, return `new String(chars)`. (Yes, `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()` also works — know both; write the manual one here.)

solution.explanation: Strings are immutable, so edit a `char[]` copy with the same two-pointer swap as arrays, then rebuild the String. O(n) time.

hints: Strings can't be edited — work on a mutable copy of the characters.
`s.toCharArray()` gives you that copy; reverse it with the two-pointer swap.
Convert back with `new String(chars)`.

title: Drill: letter frequency array
prompt: From memory: return the count of the most frequent character in `s` (lowercase letters only, non-empty). Build the `int[26]` count array, then scan it for the max.

solution.explanation: Count array + scan: the two-pass shape you'll reuse in Valid Anagram, Longest Repeating Character Replacement, and more.

hints: Two passes: first tally every letter, then find the biggest tally.
`int[] counts = new int[26];` and `counts[c - 'a']++` for each char.
Second loop over `counts` with `Math.max`.

title: Recall: conversions and Character helpers
prompt: Fill in the conversion and helper methods.
code:
int n = Integer.{{1}}("42");            // "42" -> 42
String s = String.{{2}}(42);            // 42 -> "42"
boolean keep = Character.{{3}}(c);      // letter or digit?
char lower = Character.{{4}}(c);        // 'A' -> 'a'
String csv = String.{{5}}(",", parts);  // {"a","b"} -> "a,b"
explanation: `Integer.parseInt` reads text as an int; `String.valueOf` goes the other way. `Character.isLetterOrDigit` filters out punctuation and spaces, `Character.toLowerCase` normalizes case, and `String.join(sep, parts)` is the inverse of `split`.

title: Recall: string access
prompt: Fill in the length, character, and substring operations.
code:
int n = s.{{1}}();          // string length (WITH parentheses)
char c = s.{{2}}(0);        // first character
String pre = s.{{3}}(0, 3); // first 3 chars, [0, 3)
explanation: Strings use `length()` (a method, unlike arrays); `charAt(i)` reads one char; `substring(start, end)` takes the half-open range.

title: Drill: last character
prompt: From memory: return the last character of `s` (non-empty) as a String. Use `charAt` and `length()`.

solution.explanation: Indices run 0..length()-1, so the last char is at `length() - 1`. `charAt` returns a `char`, and `String.valueOf` converts it to the required `String`.

hints: Indices start at 0, so the last one is one less than the length.
The last index is `s.length() - 1`.
`String.valueOf(char)` turns a char into a String.

title: Recall: search & split
prompt: Fill in the search and split operations.
code:
int i = s.{{1}}("b");         // first index of "b", or -1
boolean has = s.{{2}}("ab");  // is "ab" a substring?
String[] parts = s.{{3}}(" "); // break on spaces
explanation: `indexOf` returns the first position (or -1), `contains` gives a boolean, `split` breaks the string into a `String[]`.

title: Drill: count words
prompt: From memory: return the number of space-separated words in `s` (0 if empty). Use `split(" ")`.

solution.explanation: `split(" ")` returns one piece per word, so its `.length` (an array field) is the count. `"".split(" ")` returns `[""]` — one empty piece — hence the guard.

hints: Splitting gives you an array of words; you only need its size.
`s.split(" ").length` — but check what it returns for `""` first.
Guard the empty string (split would give `[""]`, length 1).

title: Recall: StringBuilder
code:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.{{1}}("ab");                 // add text
sb.{{2}}(sb.length() - 1);      // remove the last char
String out = sb.{{3}}();        // final String
explanation: `append` adds, `deleteCharAt(length-1)` pops the last char (key for backtracking), `toString` produces the final String.

title: Drill: build with StringBuilder
prompt: From memory: return the string `"ab"` repeated `n` times, built with a StringBuilder in a loop (never `+=` in a loop!).

solution.explanation: Appending into one buffer is O(total length); `+=` would recopy the growing string each time. `n = 0` never enters the loop and returns "".

hints: Use one growable buffer for the whole build instead of creating a new String each iteration.
Create the builder before the loop, `append("ab")` inside, `toString()` after.
